By Paul Shoemaker · October 27, 2026

Ghost Rivers

Finding the Gold Traps Time Left Behind

Exploring ancient waterways, glacial history, abandoned channels, and the hidden geography of placer gold.

Today's blue line on a map tells only part of a river's story. Ghost Rivers follows the evidence for earlier waterways—and asks whether any of the sediments they left behind could still hold placer gold.

Start with our first investigation: The Swift River, Maine: Searching for the Waterways That Came Before. Or open the research map and compare actual geological mapping with the modern river.

A river can leave more than one kind of memory

An abandoned bend may be comparatively recent. A stream terrace can record an older valley floor. A glacial meltwater channel belongs to a different drainage system altogether. These features should not share an age simply because they look like dry channels today.

Maine's geological survey describes glaciers eroding and transporting sediment, disrupting drainage, and leaving deposits that later rivers could rework. That gives us a process to investigate, not a ready-made reconstruction of a particular ancient river. Read the survey's glacial-history overview.

Gold concentration needs its own evidence. Warren E. Yeend's USGS placer-gold model describes several depositional settings and trapping contacts. Finding an old channel is not equivalent to finding a gold-bearing one.

Three kinds of evidence, clearly separated

Label What it means here What it does not establish
Verified geological feature A documented observation or identifiable feature, such as the published Coos Canyon bedrock locality A productive gold trap or permission to sample
Research-supported interpretation An interpretation in attributed geological mapping, such as a mapped meltwater channel An independently dated former course of the Swift River
Unverified prospecting hypothesis A proposed trapping or preservation mechanism that still needs testing Gold presence, grade, access, or profitability

Confidence describes the evidence for the stated claim. A reliable geological map can support a landform interpretation while saying nothing about gold yield.

How we look for a vanished waterway

We compare terrain, mapped sediments, dated maps and photographs, and observations of sediment contacts. A useful lead needs more than a curved hollow: roads, drainage works, lake margins, and unrelated glacial features can also produce suggestive shapes.

The Maine Geological Survey's guide to reading surficial maps explains how field observations and landform evidence inform geological interpretation. USGS topoView provides historical topographic maps. Maine's historical aerial-photo collection offers another route to dated comparisons. Those resources are investigation tools; we have not yet completed a historical image comparison for Swift River.

A practical question, rather than a promise

Could reworked older gravel preserve a trapping contact beyond today's channel? Perhaps. Establish the sediment's origin, its relationship to the river, and lawful access first. Then consider small, comparable samples where specifically permitted. Keep negative results: they are part of the research.

Research checked October 27, 2026. This is an ongoing geological investigation. No ancient river course or gold-bearing target has been invented for this project.
